questions.q: What does response.json() do on a requests Response object?
options: Always returns the HTTP status code
Converts the response into a CSV file
Parses the response body as JSON into a Python dict or list
questions.explain: It's the same underlying parsing as json.loads(), applied to the response body.

questions.q: What does a 200 status code from requests.get() mean?
options: The requested resource was not found
questions.explain: 200 is the standard HTTP success status.

questions.q: Why is checking response.status_code (or calling raise_for_status()) important before reading data from a JSON response?
options: requests.get() automatically raises an exception on every non-200 response with no extra code needed
JSON responses are never returned for failed requests
A failed request (like a 404) still returns a well-formed JSON body, so code that skips the check can crash with a confusing KeyError instead of a clear error
Status codes are only relevant for POST requests, never GET
questions.explain: A typo'd URL against GitHub's API returns a normal 404 JSON body like {"message": "Not Found"}, not a Python exception, unless you check or call raise_for_status().

options: Raises a requests.HTTPError if the response status is in the 4xx or 5xx range
Converts the status code into a string
Retries the request automatically up to 3 times
questions.explain: It's a convenient way to turn a bad HTTP status into a Python exception you can catch.

questions.q: By default, how many contributors does GitHub's contributors endpoint return per page?
options: All of them, with no limit
questions.explain: GitHub's default page size is 30 results — getting more requires pagination, covered in the next lesson.
